settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: readStartHeader consumes a fixed 20-byte CRC32-verified block (line 372-378), and readHeaders validates nextHeaderCrc against a CRC32 of the header buffer (lines 346-350) before parsing, reducing arbitrary unverified header content but not the size of sizes declared inside a CRC-valid header
readFully(buf) throws EOFException if the underlying channel is shorter than the declared nextHeaderSize, limiting some cases to an IO error rather than OOM
candidates.description: In readArchiveProperties, propertySize is read as an untrusted 64-bit uint directly from the archive header via readUint64(input), then immediately cast to int and used to allocate a byte[] (new byte[(int)propertySize]) before any bound check, stream-length check, or confirmation that the bytes exist. The subsequent input.get(property) then copies that many bytes. A crafted 7z archive can supply a large nextHeaderSize (the outer header buffer is itself allocated from startHeader.nextHeaderSize at line 344) or an oversized propertySize, causing a huge heap allocation / negative-size attempt (int truncation of a value > 2^31) that can degrade to OutOfMemoryError or NegativeArraySizeException — a denial-of-service condition when processing untrusted 7z headers. Similar int-truncating allocations exist for the folder unpack size (new byte[(int)folder.getUnpackSize()], line 444).
missing_evidence: Whether application-level limits (e.g. MemoryLimitException) are applied by callers before or around these allocations
Actual peak allocation for a crafted header in practice and whether the JVM rejects it as NegativeArraySizeException vs OOM
Whether the reference 7z format constrains propertySize relative to remaining header bytes at parse time
preconditions: Caller constructs SevenZFile over an attacker-controlled 7z stream/channel
The archive header reaches readArchiveProperties (kArchiveProperties NID) or an encoded header with a large declared unpack size
No MemoryLimitException limits are enforced on these particular allocations
candidates.title: 7z header property array allocated from untrusted uint64 before content validation

counter_evidence: supportsCompressedSizeFor and supportsDataDescriptorFor gate which entries are processed (lines 846-860); drainCurrentEntryData throws EOFException on truncated input (lines 746-748), and readFirstLocalFileHeader raises UnsupportedZipFeatureException for split markers
For non-stored deflated entries the Inflater itself bounds decompressed output to the declared uncompressed size
candidates.description: readDataDescriptor reads CRC and size fields (compressed/uncompressed) directly from the stream (ZipLong/ZipEightByteInteger), then setCompressedSize/setSize are applied to the current entry with no plausibility bounds. These attacker-controlled sizes feed later logic: for STORED entries readStored uses current.entry.getSize() as csize and loops up to that value; closeEntry/drainCurrentEntryData compute remaining = getCompressedSize() - bytesReadFromStream and loop reading from the underlying stream (line 743-752), and readStoredEntry caches stored entries with data descriptors. A crafted archive that declares an enormous compressed/uncompressed size via a data descriptor can drive large allocations or long/again-large read loops (decompression-style DoS) even though the actual data is short; the EOFException guard only triggers when the stream ends.
missing_evidence: Behavior of readStoredEntry for an oversized declared size (whether it allocates the full size up front) — file was only read through line 860
Whether typical callers wrap entries with ratio/size limits
preconditions: ZipArchiveInputStream is constructed with allowStoredEntriesWithDataDescriptor (or the entry method is DEFLATED/ENHANCED_DEFLATED which support data descriptors)
Attacker supplies a zip entry whose data descriptor advertises sizes far larger than the real payload
Caller does not enforce its own entry-size/ratio limits
candidates.title: Data-descriptor size fields from untrusted stream trusted without bounds for stored entries

counter_evidence: The surrounding code path is intended for entries with known compressed size and the skip(Long.MAX_VALUE) is documented as guaranteed to exhaust the stream (line 694-695)
getBytesInflated compensates for the 2^32 boundary to keep inB close to bytesReadFromStream (lines 770-777)
candidates.description: In closeEntry, when outstanding bytes are absent the code calls skip(Long.MAX_VALUE) to exhaust the stream, then computes diff as (int)(current.bytesReadFromStream - inB) and uses it to pushback bytes with buf.array(), buf.limit() - diff. The comment asserts diff is "at most a single read()" but the cast truncates a long difference to int; a mismatch between bytesReadFromStream and the inflater's consumed count (getBytesInflated handles the 2^32 wraparound and returns -1 for unknown methods, lines 770-777 and 494-496) could make buf.limit() - diff out of range and push back from the wrong offset. This is a correctness/robustness weakness that depends on untrusted entry metadata (compressed size, method) and could lead to reading wrong buffered bytes rather than the intended pushback.
missing_evidence: A concrete archive state that produces diff outside [0, buf.limit()]; not demonstrated by static reading
Whether any caller reaches closeEntry with an unrecognized method where current.bytesRead is 0
preconditions: An entry whose compressed size/method leads to a non-trivial difference between bytesReadFromStream and the inflated/consumed byte count
candidates.title: Read/close of zip entry relies on cast of size difference to int in pushback

counter_evidence: Lines 241-251 explicitly canonicalize both target dir and file and compare with a trailing separator, and the 1.18 changelog states the prior prefix-sibling bug was fixed
Files are opened with Files.newOutputStream without following a pre-created symlink by name only (the canonical check occurs first)
candidates.description: The example Expander (documented as a high level API for expanding archives) derives the output File directly from nextEntry.getName() (new File(targetDirectory, nextEntry.getName())) and guards only via f.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(targetDirPath). This is the same class of check that the project itself records as previously vulnerable (changes.xml: 'The example Expander class has been vulnerable to a path traversal in the edge case ... target directory has a sibling directory and the name of the target directory is a prefix of the sibling directory's name'). The current code appends File.separatorChar to targetDirPath (lines 242-244), which mitigates the specific sibling-prefix edge case, but absolute entry names, drive-letter names, or symlinked targets are still resolved through getCanonicalPath; correctness of the guard depends entirely on that canonicalization and on the platform, and there is no rejection of absolute/UNC names. Because Expander is example code widely copied, its name-handling is security-relevant.
missing_evidence: Whether symlinks inside the target directory (created by an earlier entry) can later be traversed by a subsequent entry to escape — not verified by reading
Behavior on Windows drive letters / UNC names (preserveDriveLetter handling elsewhere in the codebase)
preconditions: Application uses Expander to extract an attacker-influenced archive
An entry name resolves via getCanonicalPath to a path still under targetDirPath but pointing through a symlink or platform-specific path semantics the guard does not account for
candidates.title: Expander example writes entries using attacker-controlled names (path handling relies solely on canonical-prefix check)
